audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 1 Kings / Melakhim Aleph chapter 17, first-pass draft aligned to public-domain verse structure; formal medical, ecological, and witness audit remains required.
audit_status.review_note: Reviewed for drought proclamation, collective famine, ravens and animal agency, drying water, foreign widow, last-meal pressure, household food, child illness and death, maternal protest, bodily contact, revival, and misuse as medical procedure.

verses.restored: Elijah the Tishbite, from settlers of Gilead, said to Ahab, As YHWH lives, Divine of Israel before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years except according to my word.
Word of YHWH came to him, saying:
Go from here, turn eastward, and hide by wadi Cherith, which is before Jordan.
You shall drink from wadi, and I commanded ravens to feed you there.
He went and did according to word of YHWH. He went and lived by wadi Cherith before Jordan.
Ravens brought him bread and meat in morning and bread and meat in evening, and he drank from wadi.
After days, wadi dried because there was no rain in land.
Word of YHWH came to him, saying:
Arise, go to Zarephath belonging to Sidon, and live there. Look, I commanded a widow woman there to sustain you.
He arose and went to Zarephath. He came to entrance of city, and look, a widow woman was gathering sticks. He called to her, Please take me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.
As she went to take it, he called to her, Please take me a morsel of bread in your hand.

She said, As YHWH your Divine lives, I have no cake, only a handful of flour in jar and a little oil in jug. Look, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go and prepare it for myself and my son; we shall eat it and die.
Elijah said to her, Do not fear. Go, do according to your word, but make for me from it a little cake first and bring it to me; afterward make for yourself and your son.
For thus says YHWH, Divine of Israel: Jar of flour shall not be exhausted and jug of oil shall not lack until day YHWH gives rain upon face of ground.
She went and did according to word of Elijah. She, he, and her household ate for days.
Jar of flour was not exhausted and jug of oil did not lack, according to word of YHWH spoken by hand of Elijah.
After these matters, son of woman, mistress of house, became sick. His sickness was very severe until no breath remained in him.
She said to Elijah, What is there between me and you, man of Divine? Did you come to me to bring my wrongdoing to remembrance and kill my son?
He said to her, Give me your son. He took him from her embrace, brought him up to upper room where he lived, and laid him upon his bed.
He cried to YHWH and said, YHWH my Divine, have you also brought evil upon widow with whom I sojourn by killing her son?
He stretched himself upon child three times and cried to YHWH, YHWH my Divine, please let life/nephesh of this child return within him.
YHWH heard voice of Elijah. Life of child returned within him, and he lived.
Elijah took child, brought him down from upper room into house, and gave him to his mother. Elijah said, See, your son lives.
The woman said to Elijah, Now this I know: you are a man of Divine, and word of YHWH in your mouth is truth.

translation_notes: Elijah's drought proclamation is not a harmless display of prophetic power. Drought and famine expose children, poor households, animals, farmers, and politically powerless people to suffering.
Ravens are narrative agents supplying food. Their behavior is not a modern feeding plan, omen system, or proof that people should avoid practical provision.
The wadi dries for Elijah too. Prophetic status does not exempt him from ecological consequences.
The widow is a foreign Sidonian woman, head of her household, who names the reality of starvation. She is not a passive object sent for Elijah's convenience.

Elijah asks for food first from a woman describing a final meal for herself and her child. The power and survival pressure make this scene dangerous to use for fundraising, clergy entitlement, or demanding that poor people give away essentials.
The flour and oil story is a miracle narrative, not a promise that food will multiply if vulnerable people surrender their last resources.
The child's illness and absence of breath may describe death but is not a clinical report. The mother rejects theology that makes her remembered sin kill her son.
Elijah's bodily stretching and prayer must not be imitated as resuscitation or substituted for emergency medical care, CPR training, or professional treatment.
The mother receives her living child back and speaks the chapter's final discernment. Her testimony matters independently of Elijah's status.
safety_note: Do not use drought, famine, or a child's death to glorify prophetic power or blame victims. Do not pressure poor people to give their last food to religious leaders. Do not imitate Elijah's bodily actions as medical treatment. Center food access, ecological care, emergency medicine, maternal protest, and the dignity of the foreign widow.
